title: Supreme Court immunity ruling grants presidents broad immunity (Jul 1, 2024)
description_short: Supreme Court immunity ruling grants presidents broad immunity (Jul 1, 2024)
description_medium: On July 1, 2024, the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that former presidents have presumptive immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts, while unofficial acts are not protected on the same basis. The decision arose from Trump’s federal election-interference case and sent questions about particular conduct back for further proceedings. It did not dismiss every charge or decide the case’s factual merits.
description_long: The Supreme Court’s July 1, 2024 ruling established that a former president has absolute immunity for some core constitutional powers and at least presumptive immunity for other official acts, while unofficial conduct receives no such protection. The 6–3 decision came in Trump’s federal case concerning efforts to overturn the 2020 election. It required courts to distinguish between official presidential conduct and private or campaign conduct before deciding which allegations could proceed. The ruling therefore changed the legal framework and required further analysis of the conduct charged; it was not a finding that Trump was innocent, nor did it automatically erase every allegation. The supplied synopsis describes the decision as granting broad immunity, a characterization reflecting the dispute over its reach. The practical consequences depended on later proceedings applying the new test to specific acts. This entry records the constitutional holding and its procedural effect without implying that the Supreme Court decided the factual merits of the prosecution.
